overview:
Nicaragua is the largest country in Central America by area, a bridge of land between Honduras and Costa Rica with the Caribbean Sea on one side and the Pacific Ocean on the other. It covers about 130,000 km², roughly the size of Greece, and a chain of volcanoes marches down its Pacific side.

About 7 million people live in Nicaragua, nearly all speaking Spanish, with English Creole and Indigenous languages such as Miskito spoken along the Caribbean coast. Managua, the capital, sits on the shore of Lake Managua and has been rebuilt after earthquakes more than once. The country is a republic whose government has been led by President Daniel Ortega since 2007; opposition parties and independent news outlets say they have been heavily restricted.

Coffee, beef, sugar and gold are the main exports. Nicaragua is famous for Lake Nicaragua, a freshwater sea big enough to hold islands with their own volcanoes, and for baseball, which here beats soccer.
landAndNature: A line of about twenty volcanoes, several of them active, runs parallel to the Pacific coast; Masaya lets visitors look down into a glowing lava lake, and Cerro Negro is young enough that people sled down its black ash slopes on boards. Lake Nicaragua, or Cocibolca, is the largest lake in Central America and holds Ometepe, an island formed by two volcanoes joined at the waist. Bull sharks swim up the San Juan River into the lake, one of the few freshwater populations in the world. The Caribbean side is a wide, wet lowland of rainforest, pine savanna and lagoons, including the Bosawás reserve, one of the biggest forests north of the Amazon. Howler monkeys, jaguars, sloths and hundreds of bird species live there.
peopleAndCulture: Most Nicaraguans are mestizo, of mixed Indigenous and Spanish descent, while the Caribbean coast is home to Miskito, Mayangna, Rama, Garifuna and Creole communities with their own languages and music. Gallo pinto, rice fried with red beans, is eaten at almost every meal, often with fried plantains, cheese and a corn drink. Nacatamales, big banana-leaf parcels of corn dough, meat and vegetables, are a Sunday tradition. Baseball is the national passion, and Dennis Martínez became the first Nicaraguan to pitch a perfect game in the major leagues. Rubén Darío, born here in 1867, changed Spanish poetry forever and is honored as the country's greatest writer. Patron saint festivals fill towns with masked dancers, fireworks and marimba bands.
history: Chorotega and Nicarao peoples farmed corn around the lakes long before Spanish ships arrived in 1522. Spain ruled for 300 years; Nicaragua became independent in 1821 and joined, then left, a short-lived Central American federation. In the 1800s the route across the country was a prized shortcut between the Atlantic and Pacific. United States Marines occupied Nicaragua for much of 1912–1933, and the guerrilla leader Augusto Sandino fought them until his murder in 1934. The Somoza family then ruled as dictators for more than 40 years. The Sandinista revolution overthrew them in 1979, and a war followed through the 1980s between the Sandinista government and US-backed Contra rebels, killing tens of thousands. Elections in 1990 brought peace. Protests in 2018 were met with force and hundreds died.
funFacts: Lake Nicaragua is home to bull sharks that swim in from the sea, leaping up the rapids of the San Juan River.
People sandboard down Cerro Negro volcano, one of the youngest volcanoes in the Americas, at speeds over 80 kilometers per hour.
Baseball, not soccer, is Nicaragua's national sport, brought by American sailors and teachers in the 1800s.
Deaf children in Managua invented an entirely new sign language in the 1980s, which linguists study as a language being born.
Ometepe island is shaped like a figure eight because two volcanoes grew together in the middle of a lake.
